newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba-Bonn 97 tax income to fall below May estimate.
newsitem.headline: Buba-Bonn 97 tax income to fall below May estimate.

text.p: The German government's 1997 income from taxes will probably be even lower than the last official estimate showed, the Bundesbank said on Wednesday.
In its monthly report for August, the central bank also said Germany's tax structure had reached a "dead end" and called for fundamental reform of the system.
"Only large, sweeping tax reform can lead out of this dead end," the bank's report said.
The government's estimates, published in May, already showed tax receipts this year were likely to be 18 billion marks less than the original prediction in November.

The fresh estimates were seen as a heavy blow to the government which is battling with the costs of record unemployment and minimal economic growth as it tries to make the grade for entry into Europe's common currency, due for launch on January 1, 1999.
But the Bundesbank said that even May's already dismal tax estimate was still optimistic.

In the first half of this year, total tax income was around 2.5 percent down on the same period in 1996, the bank said, and even with a pick-up in economic growth and the increased impact of certain revenue-generating moves, receipts in the second half would not be enough to match the May estimate.
"From the current standpoint, tax receipts for 1997 will probably still be lower than the May forecast," the report said.
"(If this is so) the structural tax weakness -- clearly shown by the further decline in the tax ratio -- will be even more pronounced in 1997 than had been assumed," it added.
The 'tax ratio' is total tax collection in relation to gross national product.
Government plans to reform Germany's convoluted tax system were thwarted last month when opposition Social Democrats blocked a bill proposing 30 billion marks of tax cuts.

With Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition clinging on to only a slim majority in the lower house of parliament and the opposition SPD in no mood to ease Kohl's progress ahead of elections in 1998, any tax reform is now unlikely to materialise for at least a year.
Many independent economists and business people have sharply criticised the stalemate, saying it is hindering foreign investment and economic growth.
The Bundesbank said a fundamental revision of the income tax system should form the centrepiece of tax reform.
This should enable a sharper decline in taxation rates and an "as extensive as possible" reduction in the number of exceptions and special discounts, its report said.

"This would create the conditions for a tax system which would be more transparent and simple, which would not distort the economic layout as much, and which would render strategies for tax-evasion less attractive."
An efficient tax system would improve the allocation of productive resources, create an incentive for better economic performance and increase growth, the central bank said.
"And at the end, there are more jobs and less unemployment," it added.
